analysis.one_liner: Exempts community banks, credit unions, and savings associations with $10 billion or less in assets from all Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform regulations.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to exempt small banks from all Dodd-Frank rules died in committee after being referred to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2017 and receiving no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe away every rule written under the 2010 Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform law for banks, credit unions, and savings associations with $10 billion or less in assets. Dodd-Frank was written after the 2008 financial crisis to require banks to hold more capital, undergo regular examinations, and follow rules meant to prevent the kinds of failures that led to government bailouts. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Small and mid-sized banks, credit unions, and savings associations with up to $10 billion in assets, which would be freed from Dodd-Frank's capital, examination, and conduct-of-business requirements entirely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks with $10 billion or less in assets

how_it_helps.text: Exempts every financial institution with $10 billion or less in total consolidated assets from all regulations issued under Dodd-Frank or any amendment made by that act.

analysis.who_pays: Depositors, borrowers, and taxpayers, who would bear the risk if lightly regulated small banks took on the same kinds of risky bets that larger banks took before 2008, since deposit insurance and potential government backstops would still apply.

drawbacks.text: The blanket exemption covers every Dodd-Frank rule, including consumer protection and capital rules, rather than tailoring relief to specific requirements that burden small institutions.

Dodd-Frank was enacted in response to the 2008 financial crisis; exempting a broad class of banks from all of its rules would remove protections put in place to prevent bank failures that taxpayers ended up paying for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument that Dodd-Frank's compliance costs fall harder on small institutions than large ones, but this bill goes far beyond targeted relief by exempting small banks from every rule the law produced, including capital and consumer protections. The cost of that trade-off falls on depositors and taxpayers, who would absorb losses if lightly regulated institutions failed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Kennedy introduced the bill on April 24, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Small and mid-sized banks benefit because Dodd-Frank rules continued to apply to them; deregulation advocates lost a vehicle they had backed, while depositors and taxpayers avoided the risk of a blanket exemption.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee.

for.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out, held no markup, and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor and never advanced past committee, so no vote record exists to show where parties stood.

industries.industry: Small and mid-sized banks, credit unions, and savings associations
industries.note: These institutions would have gained the most from exemption but the bill never advanced, so their regulatory burden did not change. Had it passed, they would have been freed from Dodd-Frank's capital and consumer rules, shifting risk to depositors and taxpayers.
